Rabies in humans is 100% treatable if timely care is sought.By Mary Kate Howland Published: Jul. 16, 2026 at 4:59 PM UTCShareAdd Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on GoogleBUNCOMBE COUNTY, N.C. (FOX Carolina) - Buncombe County health officials are encouraging anyone who visited a certain wildlife rescue center in Asheville in the last six months to contact their local health department for a rabies risk assessment.Officials said that anyone who visited Michelle Cole or Alleyoop Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation in Asheville in the Sand Hill Road area of Candler and had contact with the wildlife there may need rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), depending on the nature of the exposure.In North Carolina, licensed wildlife rehabilitators must possess a Captivity License for Rehabilitation, an additional rabies vector species certification, and have a complete rabies pre-exposure series to be allowed to handle and rehabilitate animal species that are at high risk of carrying rabies virus, such as bats, raccoons, skunks, foxes and bobcats. In Buncombe County and other counties where the US Department of Agriculture’s Oral Rabies Vaccination program is conducted, the rehabilitation and release of rabies vector species is not authorized except for bats. Unlicensed individuals are not allowed to possess or provide care to wildlife due to safety and public health concerns.Officials encourage residents to do the following:Do not approach, feed, or handle wildlife. If a wild animal or stray pet near your home appears sick or is behaving unusually, or if you find a bat inside your home, contact the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission Wildlife Helpline 866-318-2401 and HWI@ncwildlife.gov or your county’s Animal Control.Keep dogs, cats, ferrets, and livestock up to date on rabies vaccinations.Do not feed pets outdoors.Supervise pets when they are outside; a fenced yard provides the best protection.Buncombe County residents who think that they may have been exposed to animals at this facility should contact Buncombe County Health & Human Services Communicable Disease staff 24/7 at 828-250-5109. Residents of other counties should contact the local health department in their county of residence. For more information on rabies prevention and wildlife, residents are encouraged to contact the NC Wildlife Resources Commission at 866-318-2401.Stay with FOX Carolina as we work to learn more.Feel more informed, prepared, and connected with FOX Carolina. news.content: Skip to contentDownload Our AppsNewsletterAdvertise With UsContact UsAbout Us61°Watertown, NYWatch LiveSend It To 7NewsWeatherSportsCommunityContestsWe the PeopleNorth Country ProfessionalsAging UntoldHomeWatch LiveElection ResultsPresidential Election MapNew York Interactive ResultsNewsHealthInterviewsObituariesYour TurnCraig's To-Do ListMilitary MattersBlast from the PastNationalMeet The TeamWeatherDelays, Closings and CancellationsSportsAthlete of the WeekCommunityNorth Country All StarsNorth Country Focus7NEWS Community CalendarChris Manning's TV DinnersMr. FoodPick-a-PetContestsNorth Country ProfessionalsCommunity Health Center of the North CountryTaylor Brothers TeamClayton Dental Office/Black River DentalTV ScheduleAbout UsMeet The TeamContact UsJob OpeningsNextGen TVCircle CountryLocal News LiveInvestigateTVWatching Your WalletPowerNationDigital MarketingGray AI PolicyRaccoon Tests Positive for Rabies in St. Lawrence County; Eighth Case This Year Close A raccoon from the DeKalb area has tested positive for rabies, according to the St. Lawrence County Public Health Department.By 7 News StaffPublished: Jul. 17, 2026 at 2:26 PM UTCShareAdd Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on GoogleWATERTOWN, New York (WWNY) - A raccoon from the DeKalb area has tested positive for rabies, according to the St. Lawrence County Public Health Department.The animal was submitted for testing by the USDA, and results were confirmed by the New York State Department of Health Wadsworth Laboratory. It is the eighth animal to test positive for rabies in St. Lawrence County so far this year.Rabies is a deadly virus spread through the saliva or brain tissue of infected animals, usually via bites or scratches. Wild animals most likely to carry the virus include raccoons, skunks, bats and foxes, but unvaccinated cats, dogs and other domestic animals can also become infected after contact with rabid wildlife.St. Lawrence County Public Health is urging residents to:Report all animal bites or possible rabies exposures to Public Health at (315) 386-2325.Keep pets and livestock up to date on rabies vaccinations, including indoor cats.Supervise pets outdoors and feed them indoors.Avoid feeding, touching or adopting wild animals or stray pets.Wash any bite or scratch wound immediately and seek medical attention if exposed to a suspected rabid animal.Reduce wildlife attractants by securing garbage, compost, birdseed and pet food.Contact an animal control officer if a wild animal is living near your home.Call your veterinarian and Public Health right away if your pet or livestock may have been exposed to a rabid animal.Wild animals may be submitted for rabies testing if they’ve had contact with people or pets, or if they’re acting strangely. Health officials say residents should safely contain the animal if possible and report the incident to Public Health.The 2026 free rabies clinic schedule is available on the St. Lawrence County website. news.content_title: Fox tests positive for rabies in Georgetown County: GCSO
news.content: GEORGETOWN COUNTY, S.C. (WCBD) – On July 16, 2026, a fox in the Georgetown County area near Plantersville Road and N Fraser Street tested positive for the rabies virus, according to the South Carolina Department of Public Health (DPH). “Due to the possibility of the spread of rabies, DPH urges you to use caution when dealing with wild or stray animals,” the department said. “If you believe you, someone you know, or your pets have come in contact with this fox or another animal that potentially has rabies, please call DPH’s Conway office at (843) 915-8801 (Option 7) during normal business hours (8:30 a.m.–5 p.m., Monday–Friday) or the DPH after-hours service number at (888) 847-0902 (Select Option 2),” the department said. DPH says if your pet is ever found with wounds of unknown origin, know that your pet could have been exposed to rabies and contact the Conway office. “This is especially important as rabies has been confirmed in your area. Take any injured pet to a veterinarian so the wounds can be treated and the administration of a rabies vaccination can be discussed,” the department said. Proof of rabies vaccination for pets (cats, dogs, and ferrets) is required by the South Carolina Rabies Control Act. “If your pet does not have a current rabies vaccination, contact a veterinarian as soon as possible for an appointment,” the department said. For more information on rabies or to find a low-cost rabies clinic in South Carolina, click here . Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. Closed Captioning Information Manage Emails Apps Careers Search Q2News/ ktvq UCN2IWwjVxh4vOnMbnjiM8Hw News Montana Politics Montana Ag Network America 250 Your Health Matters More + Indian Country Positively Montana My MTN Contests Quick Links + News Montana Politics Montana Ag Network America 250 Your Health Matters Indian Country Positively Montana My MTN Contests News Actions Facebook Tweet Email Yellowstone County reports confirmed rabies case, officials stress pet vaccinations Prev Next Photo by: Facebook Post from Billings Animal Family Hospital By: Isabel Spartz Posted 3:04 AM, Jul 13, 2026 and last updated 4:02 PM, Jul 13, 2026 BILLINGS — State officials have confirmed a case of rabies in Yellowstone County, prompting veterinarians to remind residents to avoid contact with wildlife and ensure pets are current on their rabies vaccinations.The Montana Department of Livestock confirmed the case earlier this month. It is the first confirmed case in Yellowstone County this year and the third reported statewide in 2026.Watch the story here: Yellowstone County reports confirmed rabies case, officials stress pet vaccinations 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE Dr. Edie Best, owner and lead veterinarian at Billings Animal Family Hospital, said while rabies cases remain uncommon, the disease is nearly always fatal once symptoms develop, making prevention critical."Rabies is 100% fatal," Best said. "The one vaccination that is absolutely mandatory is the rabies vaccination."Rabies is a viral disease that affects the nervous system and can spread to both animals and humans through bites or scratches from infected animals. Health officials say residents should never approach or handle wild animals, particularly species known to carry the virus, including bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes.Best said unusual behavior is often the first warning sign."If you see one of those animals out in the daytime or acting unusually, like a bat that's laying on the ground or a skunk that's out in the middle of the day, ... stay away," she said. "That's not normal."While human rabies infections are rare, any potential exposure should be treated as a medical emergency."If you get bit by that animal, that's an emergency room trip immediately," Best said. "The hard part about testing for rabies is the only way to test is to test the brain, so the animal has to be deceased."According to the Montana Department of Livestock, there have been 27 confirmed rabies detections in Montana since July 2025, all involving bats. The Yellowstone County case marks the county's first confirmed detection this year.Best said residents shouldn't panic but should remain aware of their surroundings, especially when spending time outdoors."We've always known it's out there," she said. "It's just a heads up. If you see something that really seems unusual, especially in one of those animals, it's probably not normal." news.content_title: Wild Bat Found at Safari Park Tests Positive for Rabies
news.content: Health Wild Bat Found at Safari Park Tests Positive for Rabies By Cassie N. Saunders , County of San Diego Communications Office Jul. 15, 2026 | 5:36 PM Reading Time: 2 minutes County public health officials are asking anyone who may have come into contact with a bat found Saturday, July 11 at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park to contact them after the animal tested positive for rabies. The deceased bat was found at 12:10 p.m. that day at the Oasis on the Rocks restaurant and was collected by a trained park employee. No human contact with the bat has been reported. If you or someone in your family or group had direct contact with the bat, or you know of someone who may have touched the bat, County Public Health Services urges you to call (619) 692-8499 as soon as possible. Only those who have direct contact with the bat, such as touching or holding the animal, are at risk for rabies. The bat was not one of the park’s collection animals. It was delivered to the County Public Health Laboratory on July 13 where testing confirmed it was positive for rabies. This is the 19th bat to test positive for rabies in San Diego County this year. In 2025, 21 bats tested positive. “Rabies is an extremely serious viral disease, one of the deadliest, with nearly 100% fatality if not caught early enough,” said Dr. Ankita Kadakia, County deputy public health officer. “We are investigating to ensure anyone who came into contact with the bat receives care quickly. Once symptoms start there is no treatment for rabies.” Public health officials remind residents: Do not touch bats or any wildlife. If you have direct contact with a bat, wash the exposed area with soap and seek medical advice. Rabies symptoms can take weeks to months to appear, and once symptoms begin, the disease is almost always fatal. Prompt treatment is highly effective. Rabies remains rare in humans due to prevention efforts. California’s most recent human rabies case occurred in 2024 in a Fresno County resident who was exposed to a bat in Merced County. Find more information about bats and other animal testing for rabies visit the rabies dashboard for additional information rabies view the County’s website. Bats play an important role in our local ecosystem. Many species of bats live in San Diego County, feeding on insects such as mosquitos. Other bat species feed on nectar from plants and pollinate them in the process. You may see bats occasionally around sunset when they are most active. It is important to respect wildlife and give wild animals space to play their role in our natural environment. Related: bat rabies

By: City News Service Posted 1:25 PM, Jul 17, 2026 SAN DIEGO (CNS) - San Diego County public health officials are asking anyone who may have come in contact with a bat last Saturday at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park to contact them after the animal tested positive for rabies.According to the county, the deceased bat was found 12:10 p.m. that day at the Oasis on the Rocks restaurant and was collected by a trained park employee. No human contact with the bat has been reported. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGEIf you or someone in your family or group had direct contact with the bat, or you know of someone who may have touched the bat, County Public Health Services asks you to call 619-692-8499 as soon as possible.Only those who have direct contact with the bat, such as touching or holding the animal, are at risk for rabies.According to the county, the animal was not one of the park's collection of animals. The bat was tested on July 13, when the county's public health laboratory confirmed it had rabies.This is the 19th bat to test positive for rabies in San Diego County this year. In 2025, 21 bats tested positive."Rabies is an extremely serious viral disease, one of the deadliest, with nearly 100% fatality if not caught early enough," said Dr. Ankita Kadakia, county deputy public health officer. "We are investigating to ensure anyone who came into contact with the bat receives care quickly. Once symptoms start, there is no treatment for rabies."Public health officials reminded the public to always give wildlife space -- bats are protected species, and it is illegal to kill, harm or keep them -- immediately wash any area that comes into contact with a bat and seek medical advice. Bat bites can be too small to see and any contact should be reported. Keep pets up-to-date on rabies vaccinations.Rabies symptoms can take weeks to months to appear, but once symptoms start, the disease is almost always fatal, county officials said.Luckily, exposure to humans is rare. California's most recent human rabies case occurred in 2024 in a Fresno County resident who was exposed to a bat in Merced County.Bats are most active around sunset and play a vital ecological role as pollinators and pest control.Copyright 2026, City News Service, Inc. news.content: Rabies alert: Raccoon tests positive after Snellville dog attack FOX 5 Atlanta Digital Team Tue, July 14, 2026 at 12:55 AM UTC The Brief A rabid raccoon attacked three dogs near Tree View Drive in Snellville on July 8, triggering a multiagency public health warning. Public health officials warn Snellville residents to stay away from animals behaving oddly, as the rabies virus is nearly always fatal if untreated. The three dogs involved are undergoing veterinary evaluations and strict rabies post-exposure management. SNELLVILLE, Ga. - A raccoon tested positive for rabies after a dog attack in Snellville, prompting public health officials to issue an immediate warning for residents to avoid animals behaving oddly. Rabid raccoon attack What we know A raccoon tested positive for rabies after it was attacked by three dogs on July 8 near Tree View Drive in Snellville. The three dogs involved are currently undergoing veterinary evaluation and rabies post-exposure management, according to Gwinnett County Animal Welfare and Enforcement and GNR Public Health. Officials advise all pet owners to make sure their pets are up to date on their rabies vaccinations. National Association of State Health Veterinarians guidelines state that unvaccinated dogs and cats exposed to a rabid animal must face a strict four-month quarantine and receive a vaccination one month before release. What is rabies? Dig deeper The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention notes that the rabies virus attacks the central nervous system and is almost always fatal in humans if left untreated. Early symptoms in humans include a fever, headache and general weakness or discomfort. Health officials urge anyone bitten or scratched by a stray or suspected rabid animal to seek immediate medical care and report the exposure. Unusual animal behavior can be reported to the Gwinnett Animal Welfare and Enforcement Bite Office. Public health response What we don't know Officials have not yet confirmed the current health status of the three dogs or whether they were vaccinated against rabies at the time of the confrontation. It remains unknown if any other wild animals or pets in the Snellville area were exposed to the rabid raccoon before the attack occurred. Protect your family What you can do If you are bitten or scratched by a stray or suspected rabid animal, seek medical care immediately and tell your healthcare provider about the exposure. After seeking medical treatment, contact GNR Public Health at 770-339-4260 to speak with the on-call epidemiologist. To report an animal acting strangely and request a pickup, call the Gwinnett Animal Welfare and Enforcement Bite Office at 770-339-3200, ext. 5576. The Source The information in this story was gathered from Gwinnett County Animal Welfare and Enforcement and GNR Public Health, who issued a joint public safety advisory, as well as medical data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and quarantine guidelines from the National Association of State Health Veterinarians

Woman Says AI Visual Search Helped Her Realize She’d Been Bitten by a Bat and Needed a Rabies Shot “It was lucky Google Lens told me to go to hospital — who knows what might have happened?” Laura Horton said By Vanessa Etienne Vanessa Etienne Vanessa Etienne is a Staff Writer for PEOPLE on the Health team. She joined the brand in 2021. People Editorial Guidelines Published on July 15, 2026 04:41PM EDT 1 Comment Laura Horton and the bat she found. Credit : Laura Horton/SWNS NEED TO KNOW Laura Horton used Google Lens to identify a bat she rescued and discovered potential rabies exposureThe AI tool prompted her to seek medical attention after noticing bite marks she hadn’t feltHorton hopes sharing her story raises awareness about rabies risks from wild animal encounters A woman is praising an AI tool for helping her seek life-saving treatment. In May 2026, Laura Horton — a 53-year-old personal trainer from Liverpool, England — was celebrating her birthday with a two-week vacation to Lesbos, Greece. On the fourth day of the trip, she noticed a bat was drowning in the swimming pool at the apartment complex she was staying in. Not thinking much of it, she decided to rescue the animal. “I grabbed it from the water on instinct because it was drowning — I had no idea of the risks,” she told Southwest News Service. “It sat on my hand for about 10 minutes, drying off.” “We all thought it looked cute, so I took a photo of it,” she added. The villa where Laura was bitten. Laura Horton/SWNS Our new app is here! Free, fun and full of exclusives. Scan to download now! After the bat flew away, Horton said she uploaded the photo to Google Lens — an AI tool that allows users to search what they see using their device’s camera — to figure out what species of bat it was. However, the results that came up were far from expected. “It started asking questions like, ‘Are those your hands?’ and ‘Have you washed your hands for 15 minutes after handling it?’” she recalled. “It warned me of the risk of rabies and said I wouldn’t feel a bite, as their teeth are too small.” “I thought it was all a bit dramatic,” she admitted. “But when I took a photo of my hand, I saw two tiny bite marks. I had no idea you could catch rabies from a bat.” Laura Horton holding the bat. Laura Horton/SWNS Related Stories Rabies Is Making a Comeback. Should You Be Worried? Organ Donor Unknowingly Gave Rabies to Cornea Graft Recipient as Well as Kidney Recipient Who Died Horton decided to call her healthcare provider the following day, which confirmed that she should seek medical attention. She was informed that she would need to receive the rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) to prevent the virus from reaching her nervous system. She immediately went to a local hospital, but claimed that due to the language barrier, getting proper treatment was difficult. “At first, they tried to send me away with antibiotics. I’m not sure they understood what happened,” she said. “I was sent to a travel clinic, and a nurse was furious I hadn’t been given the first dose yet. I went back to the hospital and found the infectious diseases department – they were brilliant.” Bite marks on Laura Horton’s hand. Laura Horton/SWNS Sign up for From the Editor, our free weekly newsletter from PEOPLE’s Editor-in-Chief, Charlotte Triggs. While in Greece, Horton received two more shots before returning home on June 1 and receiving a fourth dose with her own doctor. “It was lucky Google Lens told me to go to hospital – who knows what might have happened,” she told the outlet. Laura Horton on vacation. Laura Horton/SWNS Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE’s free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer​​, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. Horton said she’s been researching more about cases of rabies and is hoping that sharing her story will help others stay safe. “I read the tragic case about the boy in Canada who died after a bat landed on his face,” she said. “A lot of people aren’t aware of the dangers of these wild animals and the risks. Hopefully I can help raise awareness.” Laura Horton on vacation. Laura Horton/SWNS According to the Mayo Clinic, there’s no immediate sign that you’ve been infected with rabies, the deadly virus that’s nearly always spread to humans from contact with an infected animal. This is why doctors advise people to seek medical treatment immediately after any contact with a wild animal, and to undergo a series of rabies vaccines. Once symptoms begin to show, the condition is usually fatal. The incubation period depends on how far away from the brain the bite or scratch is, and how severe it is — and/or how much of the virus is transferred, the CDC warns. news.content: Menu Menu Home Business Politics Nigeria International 2Open submenu Health & Wellbeing Education Life & Style Sport Editorial Backpage Close submenuInternational Africa Rest of the World Sunday, 19th July, 2026 Home Business Politics Nigeria International Africa Rest of the World Health & Wellbeing Education Life & Style Sport Editorial Backpage Search for: Breaking News Breaking: Badejo-Okusanya Emerges NBA’s New National President 29 minutes ago Badejo-Okusanya Set to Emerge as NBA President 2 hours ago Breaking: Court Dashes Hope of Turaki-led PDP To Be Recognised By INEC, Dismisses Suit 2 days ago Breaking: FG Files 10-Count Charge Against Three Suspects over Oyo School Pupils, Teachers’ Abduction 2 days ago Latest Headlines betPawa Pays Out $1.6m from Its Locker Room Bonus Programme Breaking: Badejo-Okusanya Emerges NBA’s New National President Tinubu’s Upcoming Visit to Akwa Ibom Badejo-Okusanya Set to Emerge as NBA President Two Dead in FCT Rabies Outbreak Nigeria | 3 days ago Shares Share Post Email Share Share Olawale Ajimotokan in Abuja Religion& Belief Two persons have died of Rabies outbreak caused by a rabid dog bite in Abuja. The Director of Veterinary Services in the secretariat, Dr Karnak Dandam, confirmed the incident in Abuja, yesterday. The two rabies fatalities were reported in Gwagwalada and in Kwali Area Councils of the FCT out of eight cases that were recorded in two area councils. Dandam said measures were already taken to curb the spread and asked residents to report dog bites. Following the outbreak, the Agriculture and Rural Development Secretariat of the Federal Capital Territory Administration (FCTA) has urged residents of the territory to vaccinate their dogs and cats. Dandam said rabies is a deadly viral disease that attacks the central nervous system and transmitted through the bite of an infected dog or cat. He listed the symptoms of rabies in humans to include fever, headache, fatigue, and pain or tingling at the site of the bite, followed by anxiety, confusion, hallucinations and barking like a dog. Also he said infested dogs will exhibit symptoms, including excessive salivation, difficulty swallowing, hallucination, hanging jaws, aggression to the owner and a severe fear of water referred to as hydrophobia . He warned FCT residents that the virus is fatal, adding that once symptoms manifest in humans, the chances of survival is rare, adding the immediate remedy after a bite “is to initiate first aid by washing the bitten areas with soap and plenty of water and to immediately present the victim to medical personnel for treatment. He said that the reported cases were recorded in March and June, of which samples were taken to the National Veterinary Research Institute (NVRI), Vom, in Plateau for confirmation. “There are eight confirmed cases of samples taken for testing at the National Reference Laboratory, NVRI, and they came out positive. “The first samples we took to Vom this year was in March and the result came out the same month. The second samples were in early June and the result came out on June 15,” he said. He explained that the secretariat had carried out vaccination campaigns for dogs and cats across the FCT in December 2025 and January 2026, adding that the vaccines were inadequate due to shortage of the doses. Dogs He equally said that the secretariat had intensified its awareness campaigns, advising residents to confine their dogs and cats after vaccination to stop them from straying, as part of measures to prevent the spread of the virus. “The secretariat is also sensitising residents across the six area councils to take their dogs and cats to designated public and private veterinary clinics for rabies vaccination and certification. “Everybody has to restrict his or her dog and cats, so that they will not be roaming the streets and become exposed to infected rabid dogs,” he said. Dandam said that the FCT Administration had taken steps to procure the needed doses of the vaccines and would soon initiate a mass vaccination exercise in all villages and towns in the six area councils of the FCT to ensure that all dogs and cats are vaccinated in every community in the territory. “Anywhere there is a dog and a cat, we will visit, vaccinate and give the owners a certificate of vaccination and license. That’s our plan.” He urged residents to pay close attention to sudden changes in the behaviours of their dogs and cats which could be signs of rabies. “The major clinical sign that the owner will notice is that the dog that has been friendly suddenly becomes apprehensive and aggressive and starts attacking without provocation. “The first sign is that the dog will seclude itself, lay in a quiet place and will not be interested in any activity. “When the rabies gradually develops, the dog will suddenly become apprehensive and start attacking any object that it comes across, even the owner will not be spared. “As the disease advances, the dog will start roaming around with its jaw widely open, which will progress to paralysis and eventual death within 10 days of the onset of clinical signs,” he said. news.content_title: FCTA Confirms Eight Rabies Cases, Two Deaths, Issues Alert
news.content: The Federal Capital Territory Administration (FCTA) has confirmed eight rabies cases and two deaths in the territory, urging residents to vaccinate their dogs and cats to curb the virus’s spread The Agriculture and Rural Development Secretary of the FCTA confirmed the rabies outbreak on Wednesday in Abuja. The Director of Veterinary Services in the secretariat, Dr Karnak Dandam, told the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) that two persons, one in Gwagwalada and the other in Kwali Area Councils of the FCT, died from rabid dog bites. Specifically, Dandam said that eight cases were recorded, five in Gwagwalada and three in Kwali Area Councils, out of which two persons lost their lives. He said measures were already taken to curb the spread and asked residents to report dog bites. Dandam described rabies as a “deadly viral disease that attacks the central nervous system” and is transmitted through the bite of an infected dog or cat. He said that the symptoms in humans include fever, headache, fatigue, and pain or tingling at the site of the bite, followed by anxiety, confusion, hallucinations and barking like a dog. In dogs, he said the symptoms include excessive salivation, difficulty swallowing, hallucinations, hanging jaws, aggression toward the owner and a severe fear of water referred to as hydrophobia. He warned that the virus is fatal, adding that once symptoms appear in humans, survival is rare. Dandam said the immediate remedy after a bite “is to wash the bite areas with soap and plenty of water as first aid and immediately present the victim to medical personnel for treatment”. The director said that the cases were recorded in March and June, adding that samples were taken to the National Veterinary Research Institute (NVRI), Vom, in Plateau for confirmation. “There are eight confirmed cases of samples taken for testing at the National Reference Laboratory, NVRI, and they came out positive. “The first samples we took to Vom this year were in March, and the result came out the same month. “The second samples were in early June, and the result came out on June 15,” he said He explained that the secretariat had carried out vaccination campaigns for dogs and cats across the FCT in Dec. 2025 and Jan. 2026, adding, however, that the vaccines could not go round due to shortage of the doses. The director equally said that the secretariat had intensified its awareness campaigns, advising residents to confine their dogs and cats after vaccination to stop them from straying, as part of measures to prevent the spread of the virus. “The secretariat is also sensitising residents across the six area councils to take their dogs and cats to designated public and private veterinary clinics for rabies vaccination and certification. “Everybody has to restrict his or her dog and cats, so that they will not be roaming the streets and become exposed to infected rabid dogs,” he said. Dandam said that the FCT Administration has taken steps to procure the needed doses of the vaccines and would soon begin a mass vaccination exercise in all villages and towns in the six area councils of the FCT. This, according to him, is to ensure that all dogs and cats are vaccinated in every community in the territory. “Anywhere there is a dog and a cat, we will visit, vaccinate and give the owners a certificate of vaccination and license. That’s our plan,’’ he said. The director also urged residents to pay close attention to sudden changes in the behaviours of their dogs and cats, which could be signs of rabies. “The major clinical sign that the owner will notice is that the friendly dog suddenly becomes apprehensive and aggressive and starts attacking without provocation. “The first sign is that the dog will seclude itself, lie in a quiet place and will not be interested in any activity. “When the rabies gradually develops, the dog will suddenly become apprehensive and start attacking any object that it comes across; even the owner will not be spared. “As the disease advances, the dog will start roaming around with its jaw widely open, which will progress to paralysis and eventual death within 10 days of the onset of clinical signs,” he said. news.content_title: Montana Officials Warn Pet Owners To Stay Alert As Rabies Cases Rise This Summer
news.content: News Actions Facebook Tweet Email Montana Officials Warn Pet Owners To Stay Alert As Rabies Cases Rise This Summer Prev Next By: Logan Cyr Posted 10:58 PM, Jul 14, 2026 HELENA — Montana livestock officials are warning residents to stay alert for possible rabies exposure this summer as reports involving bats and other wildlife continue across the state. The Montana Department of Livestock says bats are the most common source of rabies cases in Montana, while skunks are typically linked to cases in southeastern parts of the state. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watching after the ad Visit Advertiser website GO TO PAGE “So in Montana the 2 types of wildlife that we see with rabies are skunks in the southeastern part of the state and then bats statewide,” said Dr. Emily Kaleczyc, assistant state veterinarian with the Department of Livestock. State officials say there have been three confirmed rabid bats in Montana so far this year, including cases in Yellowstone, Gallatin and Flathead counties. The department also says it receives several calls a day involving pets or people exposed to wildlife. “A lot of human exposures, especially in Montana, are related to people finding bats in homes or cabins,” Kaleczyc said. Officials say anyone who may have been bitten or exposed to a bat should contact a doctor or public health official right away. They also warn that rabies does not always cause aggressive behavior in animals. Pets or livestock infected with rabies may simply act differently than normal. “Any changes in behavior, especially anything neurologic related, can be a sign of rabies in domestic species,” Kaleczyc said. State veterinarians say keeping pets and livestock vaccinated is the best way to prevent the disease. “So we have very effective vaccines against rabies for all of our domestic species, dogs, cats, all of our livestock species,” Kaleczyc said. Officials encourage anyone with questions or concerns about possible rabies exposure to contact the Montana Department of Livestock at 406-444-2976 or visit the department’s website. (Photo: AdobeStock)Comment on this story2CommentShare storySharetopics: RabiesTehama CountyBatsPet VaccinationsPublic HealthAnimal BitePost-Exposure TreatmentCalifornia Department of Fish and WildlifeRight arrowTEHAMA — Two bats found in residential areas of Tehama County recently tested positive for rabies, prompting county health officials to remind residents to avoid contact with wild animals and ensure pets are vaccinated.The Tehama County Health Services Agency said rabies is a fatal viral disease that affects the central nervous system and can spread to humans and other mammals through the bite of an infected animal. Health officials said the disease is preventable if people take proper precautions and seek treatment promptly after a potential exposure.Officials urged residents not to handle, feed or attempt to capture unfamiliar, stray or wild animals, including bats and feral cats. Pet owners are encouraged to keep animals on a leash during outdoor activities and prevent them from interacting with wildlife.Children also should be taught not to approach unfamiliar animals, even if they appear friendly, according to the agency.Anyone bitten or scratched by an animal should immediately wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water and seek medical attention. Residents who believe they have been exposed to a potentially rabid animal should contact the Tehama County Health Services Agency Public Health Division at (530) 527-6824.Powered By 10 Sec 30.4K 2Two Tehama County bats test positive for rabies; officials urge pet vaccines and caution NextStayHealth officials also reminded pet owners to keep rabies vaccinations current through a licensed veterinarian.According to the agency, bats are the primary source of human rabies infections in the United States. While domestic animals account for fewer than 10% of reported rabies cases nationwide, rabies remains widespread among bats in Tehama County.Officials cautioned that rabid animals do not always display the commonly associated symptoms of excessive drooling or foaming at the mouth. Instead, infected animals may appear unusually aggressive or tame, stagger, become active during the day if they are normally nocturnal, or show other abnormal behavior.If left untreated, rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms develop. Early symptoms include fever, headache and fatigue before progressing to neurological symptoms such as confusion, hallucinations, difficulty swallowing and paralysis.Health officials said modern post-exposure treatment consists of four vaccine injections administered over two weeks, along with an injection of rabies immune globulin on the first day of treatment. The treatment is highly effective when started promptly after exposure.Residents who observe sick, injured or distressed wildlife are encouraged to report the animal to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife. news.content: LOCAL Rabies cases in RI are already outpacing recent years. What to know. Thirty-two humans have been exposed to rabies and received treatment in Rhode Island this year Jack Perry Providence Journal July 16, 2026, 3:13 p.m. ET Play Unmute -- / -- Full screen Keep Watching Rhode Island has seen a rise in rabies cases in 2026, surpassing the previous five-year average. State officials warn residents to avoid contact with wild animals to prevent exposure to the fatal disease. Raccoons and bats are the primary carriers of rabies identified in the state this year. An average of 24 animals in Rhode Island tested positive for rabies in each of the last five years, but 25 animals have already tested positive in 2026, with the year little more than half over. Thirty-two humans have been exposed to rabies and received treatment in Rhode Island this year, according to a joint press release from the Rhode Island Department of Health and the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management. State officials took the opportunity on Thursday, July 16, to again remind Rhode Islanders about the importance of protecting themselves against the disease, which is fatal if not treated in time. Director of Health Dr. Jerry Larkin, said, “Being active in nature regularly is one of the best things you can do for your health. However, you should never touch a wild animal. "Any contact with a wild mammal puts you at risk for rabies.” Where have rabid animals been found? Rhode Island State Veterinarian Dr. Scott Marshall said, "Any direct contact with a wild mammal should be considered a potential rabies exposure." He said people should not approach or feed wild animals and should "report animals behaving unusually to authorities.” The majority of the rabid animals caught this year have been in the northern part of the state, according to state officials. Raccoons have accounted for the most, 14, followed by bats, 7. A rabid cat, coyote, skunk and a woodchuck have also tested positive this year, officials said. Rabies is most commonly transmitted through the bite of an infected animal, but it can also spread when saliva from a rabid animal enters the body through a scratch or an open wound, according to state officials. State law requires all dogs, cats and ferrets to be vaccinated against rabies. State officials say vaccinating pets prevents them from getting rabies and prevents people from becoming exposed to rabies through their pets. The health department recommends the following additional steps to prevent rabies: Avoid all contact with and do not feed stray or free-roaming domestic animals. Avoid all contact with and do not feed wild animals. Do not feed your animals outdoors, as this will attract other animals. This is especially dangerous when feeding large numbers of free-roaming cats. Protect your pets by always maintaining control; walk dogs on a leash or let them play in a fenced yard; and do not let pets wander unsupervised. Securely cover all garbage cans so wild animals cannot scavenge for food. What to do if a person or pet comes into contact with a wild animal Anyone who has had direct contact with a wild mammal should immediately call RIDOH's Center for Acute Infectious Disease Epidemiology at 401-222-2577 (Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. or 401-276-8046 after hours). A RIDOH nurse will assess the exposure and determine whether post-exposure treatment is recommended. If needed, RIDOH will coordinate a post-exposure vaccine series. If any domestic animal, such as pets or livestock, had contact with a wild mammal, or if you are in possession of an animal that you suspect has rabies, call RIDOH, your local animal control officer, and your veterinarian. What a doctor says 'Boo Boo' Andrade eyes comeback after family tragedy Bats sometimes get inside homes, and testing of the bat or preventive vaccination is recommended when a bat has been found in a home where people or pets have been sleeping, or if the bat was around people who do not know if they had contact with the bat. For more information on how to prevent rabies, visit RIDOH’s website. For more information on rabies and ways to protect yourself and your pets, please see this RIDOH fact sheet. news.content_zh: 罗德岛州本地狂犬病病例数量已超过近年来。今年,罗德岛州已有 32 人接触过狂犬病并接受治疗 Jack Perry Providence Journal 2026 年 7 月 16 日下午 3:13 ET Play Unmute -- / -- 全屏继续关注 罗德岛州 2026 年狂犬病病例有所增加,超过了之前五年的平均水平。州官员警告居民避免接触野生动物,以防止感染这种致命疾病。浣熊和蝙蝠是该州今年发现的狂犬病的主要携带者。过去 5 年,罗德岛州平均每年有 24 只动物狂犬病检测呈阳性,但到 2026 年,已有 25 只动物检测出狂犬病呈阳性,而这一年仅过半。根据罗德岛州卫生部和罗德岛州环境管理部的联合新闻稿,今年罗德岛州已有 32 人感染狂犬病并接受治疗。

Raccoons Test Positive for Rabies in July; 8 Total this Season July 13, 2026 Sophia Peters, UPDATE: The Wicomico County Health Department has announced two more positive rabies cases found in raccoons this July, making the total number of positive cases eight this year. On Jul. 2, a raccoon tested positive for rabies in the area of Nithsdale on Caledonia Drive in Salisbury. Less than two weeks later, on Jul. 13, another raccoon tested positive for rabies; this time in the area of Archie Dennis Road in Parsonsburg after contact with a dog. The Wicomico County Health Department continues to advise all residents to be aware of their surroundings and avoid contact with all wild and/or stray animals. UPDATE: The Wicomico County Health Department (WCHD) has announced that another raccoon has tested positive for rabies, making it the fifth rabies case in Wicomico this year. On Friday, Jun. 12, a raccoon tested positive for rabies in the area of Kensington Woods and Upper Ferry Road in Salisbury Maryland, after contact with a dog. The Wicomico County Health Department is advising all residents to be aware of their surroundings and avoid contact with all wild and/or stray animals. This update was published on Ju. 12 at 5:00 p.m. UPDATE: The Wicomico County Health Department (WCHD) has announced that another raccoon has tested positive for rabies, making it the fourth case in the county in just two months. On Tuesday, Apr. 28, a raccoon tested positive for rabies in the area of Hazel Street and Old Ocean City Road in Salisbury after having contact with a dog. The Wicomico County Health Department is advising all residents to be aware of their surroundings and avoid contact with all wild and/or stray animals. This update was published on Apr. 28 at 3:28 p.m. WILLARDS, Md. – The Wicomico County Health Department (WCHD) has announced that a third raccoon in the county has tested positive for rabies. Officials say the raccoon was found near in the area of Rayne Road in Willards after it had contact with a dog. Two other rabid raccoons were located this month in Parsonsburg and Delmar. The WCHD is advising all residents to be aware of their surroundings and avoid contact with wild/stray animals. They also offer the following tips to protect your family and pets: Keep pets confined and avoid feeding them outside Teach children to leave unfamiliar animals alone Vaccinate pets Secure outside garbage bins Rabies is a preventable viral disease that exists in and is transmitted by the saliva of mammals. Maryland law requires all dogs, cats, and ferrets aged four months or older to have a current rabies vaccination. If left untreated, rabies is fatal. To report human or animal contact, such as bites or scratches, call WCHD at (410)-546-4446. officials urge pet vaccinesby News StaffMon, July 13, 2026 at 3:34 PMUpdated Tue, July 14, 2026 at 10:05 AM(File: Getty Images)Comment on this story0CommentShare storySharetopics: RabiesLane CountyPublic HealthBatPet VaccinationOregonVeterinary Diagnostic LaboratoryRabies PreventionRight arrowEUGENE, Ore. — Lane County Public Health (LCPH) on Monday announced laboratory confirmation from the Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory at Oregon State University of a rabies-infected bat found in Lane County. This is the third bat found in Lane County which has tested positive for rabies in 2026."All pet owners should make certain their dogs and cats are vaccinated against rabies. When our pets are protected from rabies, it provides a buffer zone of immune animals between humans and rabid wild animals, such as bats," says Dr. Emilio DeBess, State Public Health Veterinarian.RELATED | Rabid bat found in Marion County prompts county health warningWhile bats help control insect populations, including mosquitoes, they are the primary reservoir of rabies in our wild animal communities, the county explained. Thus far this year in Oregon 13 bats have tested positive for rabies.Third rabies-positive bat found in Lane County this year; officials urge pet vaccinesLane County residents and veterinarians should be aware that other animals could be exposed to the rabies virus and should, therefore, be alert to potential signs of the disease. Rabies is a viral disease that affects the nervous system of humans and mammals. It is almost 100 percent fatal once symptoms begin. The virus is carried in the saliva of an infected animal; transmission can occur when that animal bites, or in rare instances, scratches another animal or person. If bitten by a bat the wound should be immediately and thoroughly cleaned with soap and water. In addition, medical attention should be sought. Finally, if easily accomplished, the bat should be captured and the event reported to the Lane County Public Health.Powered By 1034 0Sunshine & 90s in the ValleysShareNextStayThere are several strains of rabies found in the U.S. (e.g., bat, skunk, fox, raccoon) but only bat rabies is found in Oregon. Other animals that have tested positive for rabies in Oregon have contracted it from bats. People should stay away from bats and not handle them.LCPH recommends the following:Vaccinate your pets (dogs and cats) against rabiesDo not handle bats with bare handsWatch wildlife from a distance. Do not approach or attempt to handle wild animals.Do not feed wild animalsKeep garbage in secure containers and away from wildlifeFeed pets indoorsSeal openings in attics, basements, porches, sheds, barns and screen chimneys that might provide access to bats and other wildlifeIf your pet has contact with a bat, contact your veterinarianComment with BubblesBE THE FIRST TO COMMENTFor a statewide map showing the distribution of rabies in bats for 2026, see below:Click here to view the PDF file by Taboolaby TaboolaSPONSORED CONTENTTimeshare Resorts Forced To Refund Owners - Is Yours On the List?SilverPenny | SponsoredSponsoredUndoJust Add 1 Drop Of This Household Item To Any Dark Spot and Wait 3 MinutesGundry MD | SponsoredSponsoredUndoAsk a Pro: "I'm 65 With $1.1M Saved. news.content: nawaiwaqt group News Paper & TV Channel Roznama Nawaiwaqt Waqt News TV Magazines Sunday Magazine Family Magazine Nidai Millat Mahnama Phool Sunday, July 19, 2026 e-Paper Today's Paper EDITOR'S PICKS Newspaper Picks OPINION Editorials Columns Letters NEWS Latest Headlines Top Stories National Sports Lifestyle & Entertainment Business International Editor's Picks Snippets Lahore Karachi Islamabad MULTIMEDIA News In Pictures Cartoons Videos BLOGS Blogs Write for Us AI Use Policy CONNECT WITH US Get Alerts Health minister approves national rabies control framework Web Desk 2:39 PM | July 13, 2026 National Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Twitter ISLAMABAD: Federal Minister for National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination Mustafa Kamal on Monday voiced serious concern over the increasing number of rabies cases and dog bite incidents across Pakistan, calling for urgent nationwide measures to tackle the preventable yet deadly disease. The minister made the remarks during a meeting with a delegation from the Indus Hospital & Health Network (IHHN), led by its Chief Executive Officer Dr Abdul Bari Khan, to discuss a comprehensive national strategy for rabies prevention and control. During the meeting, the delegation briefed the minister on the country's rabies situation, highlighting the absence of an effective national rabies surveillance system. FFD issues high flood alert for Chenab, Jhelum rivers According to estimates shared during the briefing, around 5,000 people die from rabies each year in Pakistan, while hundreds of thousands of dog bite cases are reported annually. Children and residents of rural and underserved urban areas are among the most vulnerable. Expressing deep concern over the growing burden of the disease, Mustafa Kamal gave in-principle approval for the development of a National Rabies Prevention and Control Framework aimed at strengthening prevention, surveillance and response efforts across the country. He also announced the formation of a National Technical Working Advisory Group, which will lead the preparation of the framework and coordinate nationwide efforts to combat rabies. Man arrested after firing incident near Attaullah Tarar's vehicle in Lahore The health minister stressed the need for a nationwide public awareness campaign to educate citizens about rabies prevention, the importance of seeking immediate medical treatment after animal bites, and timely vaccination. During the meeting, Dr Abdul Bari Khan presented the minister with the "Sindh Official Guidelines for Prevention of Human Rabies (2024)," developed with the technical assistance of The Indus Hospital and Health Network. The meeting was held days after another rabies case was reported in Karachi. On July 10, a 28-year-old woman, identified as Malookan Bibi from Khwaja Ajmer Nagri in North Karachi, was admitted to the emergency department of Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre (JPMC) after developing symptoms of the fatal viral disease. news.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Wildfire Smoke World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Atlanta | News Weather Meet Our Team News Tips 76° Contact Us Download Our App Advertise Memorials Watch CBS News Local News Raccoon attacked by dogs tests positive for rabies in Snellville area, officials say By Dan Raby Dan Raby Senior Digital Producer, CBS News Atlanta Dan Raby, the senior digital producer for CBS News Atlanta, has been covering everything happening around Georgia for more than a decade. Read Full Bio Dan Raby July 13, 2026 / 1:10 PM EDT / CBS Atlanta Add CBS News on Google A raccoon that had been attacked by multiple dogs last week has tested positive for rabies, Gwinnett County officials say.Authorities say the attack happened on July 8 near Tree View Drive in Snellville.The three dogs involved in the attack are now undergoing evaluation and rabies post-exposure management by veterinarians. Georgia is a rabies-endemic state, which means the virus can be found in wildlife year-round. Officials say that means it's important for residents to make sure their pets are up-to-date on their vaccinations and avoid animals that may be behaving in unusual ways. In June, a raccoon in the Bethlehem area of Gwinnett County tested positive for rabies.The National Association of State Health Veterinarians says all unvaccinated dogs and cats exposed to a rabid animal need to be quarantined for four months and vaccinated one month before being released.If you have been bitten or scratched by any stray animals or an animal suspected to have rabies, seek medial care immediately and let your provider know about the possible exposure. After that, contact GNR Public Health at (770) 339-4260 and ask for the on-call epidemiologist.To report an animal behaving in an unusual way, call the Gwinnett Animal Welfare and Enforcement Bite Office at (770) 339-3200, ext. 5576. By 828newsNOW July 16, 2026 3:23 pm Facebook X More LinkedIn Email SMS Associated PressAP Photo/Hans Pennink, FileFILE - Oral rabies vaccine bait that will be dropped by a state police helicopter from the New York State Police Aviation Unit in Albany and team members of the State Health Department is displayed during a rabies vaccine bait drop over the Northeastern part of the state during the New York State Department of Health Racoon Vaccination Project, Monday, Aug. 20, 2007. The U.S. government has begun scattering millions of packets of oral rabies vaccine from helicopters and planes over 13 states from Maine to Alabama. The major aim is to keep raccoons from spreading their strain of the deadly virus to states where it hasn't been found or isn't widespread, said field trial coordinator Jordona Kirby. CANDLER, N.C. (828newsNOW) — Local health officials have advised anyone who has visited Alleyoop Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation, an Asheville-area animal rescue, within the past six months to seek a rabies risk assessment. Buncombe County officials alerted visitors to Michelle Cole or Alleyoop Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation, located in the Sand Hill Road area of Candler, that they should contact their local health department for a rabies risk assessment if they have visited the practice or had contact with wildlife there since February 2026. “In the State of North Carolina, licensed wildlife rehabilitators must possess a Captivity License for Rehabilitation, an additional rabies vector species certification and have a complete rabies pre-exposure series to be allowed to handle and rehabilitate animal species that are at high risk of carrying rabies virus,” Buncombe County said in a press release. Rabies-carrying species include: Bats Bobcats Foxes Raccoons Skunks In Buncombe County, and other counties where the United States Department of Agriculture Oral Rabies Vaccination program is enacted, rehabilitating and releasing those vector species is not authorized, with the exception of bats. “Unlicensed individuals are not allowed to possess or provide care to wildlife due to safety and public health concerns,” the county said. Officials advise the following precautions for preventing rabies exposure: Do not approach, feed or handle wildlife. Leave orphaned wildlife alone. If a wild animal or stray pet near your home appears sick or is behaving unusually, or if you find a bat inside your home, contact the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission Wildlife Helpline at (866) 318-2401 and HWI@ncwildlife.gov, or your county animal control. Keep dogs, cats, ferrets and livestock up to date on rabies vaccinations. Do not feed pets outdoors. Supervise pets when they are outside. A fenced yard provides the best protection. If you think you have been exposed to animals at this facility, contact the Buncombe County Health & Human Services – Communicable Disease staff at (828) 250-5109. Residents of other counties should contact the local health department in their county of residence. For more information on rabies prevention and wildlife, residents are encouraged to contact the NC Wildlife Resources Commission at (866) 318-2401. Facebook X More LinkedIn Email SMS That cool break was short-lived: Asheville’s heat returns this week Asheville will see highs near 90 degrees, with afternoon thunderstorms possible Friday through Sunday By Dee Pridgen July 16, 2026 12:31 pmSponsored by Precision International Facebook X More LinkedIn Email SMS ContributedSpecial to 828newsNOWSunset Thursday near Alexander. ASHEVILLE, N.C. (828newsNOW) — After a brief break from the summer heat, warmer temperatures are returning to Western North Carolina. Highs are expected to climb back into the upper 80s and low 90s this week, with heat index values approaching triple digits in parts of the region. The National Weather Service Greenville-Spartanburg office said hot conditions will return Thursday and continue through the weekend. While mountain valleys, including Asheville, are expected to stay a little cooler than areas farther east, temperatures will still run above normal. Thursday’s forecast for Asheville calls for mostly sunny skies with a high near 90 degrees. Temperatures will increase slightly Friday, with a high near 91 and a chance of afternoon showers and thunderstorms. The hottest conditions are expected across the Piedmont and foothills, where heat index values could reach 100 to 105 degrees from Thursday through Sunday. Forecasters said heat advisories could become possible, especially in areas farther east. The weather service is reminding people to take precautions during the heat, including staying hydrated, limiting strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest part of the day and checking on vulnerable neighbors and family members. A cold front moving in from the north could bring some relief early next week. Before then, rain chances will increase over the weekend. Asheville has an 80 percent chance of showers and thunderstorms Saturday, with additional chances Sunday afternoon. Temperatures are expected to ease slightly, with highs in the upper 80s to near 90 through the weekend. Forecasters said storms will be most likely during the afternoon and evening hours, especially across the mountains. Some storms could bring heavy rain, gusty winds or isolated severe weather. The return of hot weather comes as the region remembers another extreme weather event. The National Weather Service noted that 110 years ago this week, the Great Flood of 1916 devastated parts of Western North Carolina. Widespread flooding and debris flows were reported throughout the French Broad River basin, and the state’s record for 24-hour rainfall was set when Altapass in Mitchell County recorded 22.22 inches of rain. news.content: LOCAL Raccoon tests positive for rabies in Whitesboro Casey Pritchard Utica Observer Dispatch July 16, 2026, 4:32 p.m. ET Unmute -- / -- Full screen Keep Watching The raccoon was sent to the New York State Department of Health Wadsworth Center for testing on July 15 and positive results were reported on July 16. Anyone who sees an animal, wild or stray, with these signs are advised not approach it and stay away. If any animal is acting strangely, call the local animal control officer for help. A raccoon has tested positive for rabies in Whitesboro and the public is advised to take precautions and make sure their pets rabies vaccinations are up to date, according to a statement from the Oneida County Health Department. The raccoon was sent to the New York State Department of Health Wadsworth Center for testing on July 15 and positive results were reported on July 16. Two humans were exposed to the raccoon. Signs of rabies Signs of rabies include: Animal acting strangely Animal acting mad Animal acting shy Animal getting unusually close Drooling or foaming from the mouth Animals: Utica Zoo asks public for help naming new peacocks Infrastructure: Mohawk Valley Water Authority gets $11M grant for lead lines Law Enforcement: State Police conducting dive operations in Mohawk River Per New York State Public Health Law, all dogs, cats, and ferrets must be vaccinated for rabies by 4 months-old and then one year following the initial dose. For more information on rabies prevention, visit oneidacountyny.gov/rabies . Those with questions or are concerned about a possible rabies exposure are advised to contact the Oneida County Health Department at 315-798-5064, available 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. news.content_title: First Ottawa County rabies case of the year found in bat
news.content: HOLLAND TOWNSHIP, Mich. (WOOD) — The first Ottawa County animal case of rabies this year has been discovered after a bat tested positive for the disease Wednesday. The Ottawa County Department of Public Health did not specify where or when the bat was found, saying only it had been informed of the positive rabies test Wednesday. As of Monday, 21 cases of rabies have been found in bats across the state, with only one case of rabies being a skunk found in Oakland County, state data shows . No humans have contracted rabies in Michigan yet this year. The risk of exposure to rapid bats is higher from May through September when bats are most active. Health officials say to never touch or handle wild animals and urge people to vaccinate their pets against rabies. Exposure to rabies happens when people or pets are scratched or bitten by a rabid animal. Animals with rabies do not always appear sick and animals suspected of having rabies should be sent in for lab testing. If you believe you have found an animal that has rabies, contact the Ottawa County Department of Public Health or your local pest control. You can also bring an animal to the Harbor Humane Society for testing if you are able to catch it without making physical contact. If you suspect that you have been exposed to a rabid animal, even while asleep, you should seek treatment immediately, health officials say. Pets who have been exposed to a rabid animal should also receive veterinary care even if they are vaccinated against the disease. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. KLCC Published July 13, 2026 at 3:56 PM PDT Twitter LinkedIn Email Michael Durham / Oregon Department of Fish and WildlifeBats are the primary rabies vector species in the U.S. Note: the bat pictured here is not sick. Lane County Public Health announced Monday that they found a rabies-infected bat. This is the third bat found in Lane County this year to test positive for the virus.Rabies is a deadly disease caused by a virus that attacks the nervous system. The virus is spread through the saliva of animals, and sometimes scratches.Animals other than bats could be exposed to rabies, and LCPH is urging pet owners to make sure their animals are vaccinated against the virus.Residents should also look out for signs of the disease, such as aggression, disorientation or excessive drooling.Other recommendations include keeping distance from wild animals, storing garbage in secure containers and sealing openings in your home that wildlife may be able to access. news.content: San Marcos fox tests positive for rabies Editor's note: The video above is previous coverage from April 7, 2026. AUSTIN (KXAN) — A report to San Marcos Animal Services said a fox with rabies attacked a stray cat on July 11 in Willow Creek Estates, according to a release. The fox was captured, but Animal Services could not find the cat, which was described as having short, black and white hair with a wound to its hindquarters. Officials said they aren't sure if the cat is owned or has any history of rabies vaccination. Officials said the cat ran into the greenbelt between the Willow Creek Estates and the Siesta Verde neighborhood. Animal Services has not been able to find the cat since the day of the fox attack. It is unknown if the cat is owned or has a rabies vaccination. Rabies is a deadly virus that is spread through a bite and can infect mammals, including wildlife, pets, and humans. Wild animals that appear to be sick, or any physical contact with a wild animal, should be immediately reported to Animal Protection Officers by contacting Animal Services at 512-805-2655. A report from Animal Services encouraged pet owners in the community to vaccinate their pets against rabies. For resources and information about obtaining low-cost rabies vaccinations for pets, visit www.sanmarcostx.gov/pethelp. Any cat matching the description should be immediately reported to Animal Services at 512-805-2655 to help stop the spread of the virus. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. news.content_title: Rabies-Infected Bat Found At San Diego Zoo Safari Park
news.content: Community Corner Rabies-Infected Bat Found At San Diego Zoo Safari Park The bat is the 19th to test positive for rabies this year in San Diego County. ESCONDIDO, CA — A wild bat found at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park tested positive for rabies, prompting county health officials to ask anyone who may have had contact with the animal to come forward. The deceased bat was found at 12:10 p.m. Saturday at the Oasis on the Rocks restaurant at the Escondido-based park. The animal was collected by a trained Safari Park employee. No human contact with the bat has been reported. The bat was not part of the park's animal collection. It was sent to the San Diego County Public Health Laboratory on Monday, where testing confirmed it had rabies. Find out what's happening in San Diegofor free with the latest updates from Patch. Anyone who touched the bat, or knows someone who may have, was urged to call County Public Health Services at 619-692-8499. Officials said only people who had direct contact with the animal are considered at risk. The bat is the 19th to test positive for rabies this year in the county. In 2025, 21 bats tested positive. Find out what's happening in San Diegofor free with the latest updates from Patch. "Rabies is an extremely serious viral disease, one of the deadliest, with nearly 100% fatality if not caught early enough," said Dr. Ankita Kadakia, the county's deputy public health officer. "We are investigating to ensure anyone who came into contact with the bat receives care quickly. Once symptoms start there is no treatment for rabies." Health officials reminded residents not to touch bats or other wildlife. Anyone who has direct contact with a bat should wash the area with soap and seek medical advice. Rabies symptoms can take weeks or months to appear, but treatment is highly effective when started before symptoms begin. Once symptoms develop, the disease is almost always fatal, officials said. (Photo courtesy of Wikimedia Commons/NIAID) Health Jul 15, 2026 – 9:29 am EDT Rabies remains ‘threat’ in Pangnirtung with multiple dogs, fox infected Nunavut government issues warning after fourth dog suspected to have disease is killed By Nunatsiaq News Anybody in Pangnirtung who had contact with a loose, large black and white husky last Friday should be seen by a nurse and assessed for rabies, says Nunavut’s Department of Health. The department issued a public service announcement Wednesday after the husky was killed Saturday for showing signs of the disease. The dog was “not available” to be tested, the public service announcement said. This is the fourth dog to show signs of rabies since May. The three other dogs tested positive for the disease, as has one fox. “Rabies remains an active and serious threat in the community,” the announcement said. Rabies is a viral disease that is almost always fatal if left untreated. Signs of rabies in animals includes strange or aggressive behaviour, staggering, frothing at the mouth, choking and making strange noises. “Wild animals infected with rabies may also appear friendly and approach humans without fear,” the announcement said. “This is abnormal behaviour for wild animals. Animals exhibiting these signs should be avoided and reported to the environmental health officer or the conservation officer.” Anybody who is bitten or scratched by an animal behaving this way should go to the health centre immediately, as treatment should be started quickly after exposure, the announcement said. The Department of Health is also urging people in Pangnirtung to keep their dogs tied up and to monitor them for signs of rabies. Privacy Policy Accept Deny Non-Essential Lake George officer gets rabies shot after dead beaver scratch News Staff WNYT Updated: July 14, 2026 - 6:18 PM Published: July 14, 2026 - 12:46 PM Lake George (File / WNYT) LAKE GEORGE, N.Y. (WNYT) – A Lake George marine patrol officer got a preventive rabies shot after being scratched by a dead beaver that later tested negative, according to the Lake George Park Commission. The Lake George Park Commission said the scratch happened Friday, July 10, while a marine patrol officer was removing an already deceased beaver from Lake George near Glen Island. “Out of an abundance of caution, the officer received a rabies vaccination as a preventative against potential infection. The recovered animal ultimately tested negative for rabies,” the commission said. (An earlier version of this story wrongly stated the marine patrol officer was attacked by a rabid beaver. NewsChannel 13 apologizes for the error.) news.content: Health & Fitness Rabid Animals In RI Prompt Officials To Share Prevention Methods More rabid animals have already turned up in Rhode Island this year than the national average, including 14 raccoons. More rabid animals have already turned up in Rhode Island this year than the annual average, including 14 raccoons, according to two state agencies. "In response to the increased number of rabid animals identified in Rhode Island this spring and summer, the Rhode Island Department of Health (RIDOH) and the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management (DEM) are reminding all Rhode Islanders to take steps to protect themselves, their families, and their pets from rabies," the two agencies said in a media release. The yearly average of 24 rabid animals between 2021 and 2025 has already been eclipsed in 2026. In addition to the 14 raccoons, the rabid animals identified were seven bats, a cat, a coyote, a skunk and a woodchuck. Find out what's happening in Across Rhode Islandfor free with the latest updates from Patch. "Rabies is a viral disease that affects all mammals, including people, and is almost always fatal once symptoms develop," the release said. "However, it is preventable if medical care is received promptly after an exposure. The virus is most commonly transmitted through the bite of an infected animal, but it can also spread when saliva from a rabid animal enters the body through a scratch or an open wound." The department of health recommended the following rabies prevention methods: Find out what's happening in Across Rhode Islandfor free with the latest updates from Patch. - Avoid all contact with and do not feed stray or free-roaming domestic animals. - Avoid all contact with and do not feed wild animals. - Do not feed your animals outdoors, as this will attract other animals. This is especially dangerous when feeding large numbers of free-roaming cats. - Protect your pets by always maintaining control. Walk dogs on a leash or let them play in a fenced yard. Do not let pets wander unsupervised. - Securely cover all garbage cans so wild animals cannot scavenge for food. See also: Get more local news delivered straight to your inbox. selected_identity.page_title: Rabid Animals In RI Prompt Officials To Share Prevention Methods

analysis.time: The news was published on 2026-07-17. The event involves rabid animals identified in Rhode Island during the spring and summer of 2026, with the yearly average of 24 rabid animals between 2021 and 2025 already being eclipsed in 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The affected population includes all Rhode Islanders, their families, and their pets. The affected animals include 14 raccoons, seven bats, a cat, a coyote, a skunk, and a woodchuck.
analysis.event: The Rhode Island Department of Health (RIDOH) and the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management (DEM) issued a media release to remind residents about rabies prevention methods in response to an increased number of rabid animals identified in the state this spring and summer.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The number of rabid animals in Rhode Island in 2026 has already exceeded the yearly average of 24 between 2021 and 2025. Rabies is a viral disease that affects all mammals, including people, and is almost always fatal once symptoms develop, though it is preventable if medical care is received promptly after an exposure.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Rhode Island Department of Health and the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management have issued official guidance on rabies prevention. The guidance includes recommendations to avoid contact with stray or free-roaming domestic and wild animals, secure garbage cans, and keep pets under control. The source is a full original report body.

analysis.brief_en: Rhode Island health officials have issued a public reminder to residents about rabies prevention following an increase in rabid animals this year. The Rhode Island Department of Health and the Department of Environmental Management reported that 14 raccoons and other animals have tested positive for rabies, surpassing the yearly average of 24 between 2021 and 2025. Officials emphasized that rabies is a fatal viral disease affecting all mammals but is preventable with prompt medical care after exposure. The guidance advises avoiding contact with stray or wild animals, securing garbage cans, and keeping pets under control to reduce the risk of infection.

Officials emphasized that rabies is a fatal viral disease affecting all mammals but is preventable with prompt medical care after exposure. The guidance advises avoiding contact with stray or wild animals, securing garbage cans, and keeping pets under control to reduce the risk of infection.

news.content_zh: 由于今年狂犬病动物数量增加,罗德岛州卫生官员向居民发出有关狂犬病预防的公众提醒。罗德岛州卫生部和环境管理部报告称,有 14 只浣熊和其他动物狂犬病检测呈阳性,超过了 2021 年至 2025 年期间 24 只的年平均水平。官员强调,狂犬病是一种致命的病毒性疾病,影响所有哺乳动物,但在接触狂犬病后通过及时医疗护理是可以预防的。该指南建议避免接触流浪动物或野生动物,保护好垃圾桶,并控制宠物以降低感染风险。

news.content: Raccoon tests positive for rabies in Greenbrier County Updated Thu, July 2, 2026 at 7:29 PM UTC CRAWLEY, WV (WVNS) — A raccoon found in the Crawley area of Greenbrier County tested positive for rabies, according to the Greenbrier County Health Department . Both the CDC the Health Department have provided residents with tips and steps to protect their families, pets and homes. According to both organizations the three key steps to rabies prevention are as follows: Making sure your pets are up to date on their vaccinations Giving wild animals adequate space Securing your home of trash or anything else that could attract unwanted wildlife If bitten or scratched, immediate cleaning of the wound for at least 15 minutes is necessary. It is also important to seek immediate medical attention from a hospital or other healthcare provider. The Greenbrier County Health Department closed the statement by saying that rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is “highly effective” if given as soon as possible. news.content: HEALTHCARE Third Lane County bat tests positive for rabies, officials warn Alan Torres Eugene Register-Guard July 13, 2026, 3:39 p.m. PT Keep Watching A bat found in Lane County tested positive for rabies , and it's the third one so far this year, Lane County Public Health warned July 13. In the announcement, county and state officials urged members of the public to vaccinate their dogs and cats against rabies if they haven't already. "All pet owners should make certain their dogs and cats are vaccinated against rabies. When our pets are protected from rabies, it provides a buffer zone of immune animals between humans and rabid wild animals, such as bats," said Dr. Emilio DeBess, state public health veterinarian. Thirteen bats have tested positive for rabies in Oregon so far this year. Rabies is a viral disease that affects the nervous system of humans and mammals. It is "almost 100 percent" fatal once symptoms begin, the county said. The virus is carried in the saliva of an infected animal and can be transmitted when that animal bites, or in rarer instances, scratches another animal or person. If you or your pet is bitten by a bat, you should thoroughly clean the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention, report the event to Lane County Public Health and, if possible, capture the bat so it can be tested. There are several strains of rabies found in the U.S. but only bat rabies is found in Oregon. Other animals that have tested positive for rabies in Oregon contracted it from bats. According to Lane County, people should stay away from bats and not handle them. Alan Torres covers local government for the Register-Guard. news.source_body_en: A fox in Georgetown County, South Carolina, tested positive for rabies on July 16, 2026, according to the South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control (DHEC) and local media. The animal was located near Plantersville Road and N Fraser Street. This is the first confirmed rabies case reported in the area for 2026. Health officials are investigating and may issue public health advisories, though specific response measures were not detailed in the report. No human or domestic animal exposures have been reported in the supplied evidence.
news.content_zh: 据南卡罗来纳州健康与环境控制部 (DHEC) 和当地媒体报道,南卡罗来纳州乔治敦县的一只狐狸于 2026 年 7 月 16 日检测出狂犬病呈阳性。该动物位于 Plantersville Road 和 N Fraser Street 附近。这是该地区 2026 年报告的第一例狂犬病确诊病例。卫生官员正在进行调查,并可能发布公共卫生建议,但报告中没有详细说明具体的应对措施。所提供的证据中没有报告人类或家畜接触的情况。
